introduction-terraform-is-a-plugin-syste.core: Terraform core is a graph engine that knows nothing about any API. Every resource type comes from a provider: a separate Go binary that core launches and talks to over gRPC. If your internal platform, SaaS tool or on-prem system has an API but no provider, you can write one and manage it with the same plan/apply workflow as AWS.

first_principles.problem: An internal DNS service is managed by tickets because there's no Terraform provider for it.
truths: Any CRUD API can be modelled.
derivation: Identify the API's **resources** and their **CRUD** calls.
Publish to a **private or public registry**.

analogy.title: A universal remote with downloadable codes
analogy.story: The remote (core) works with any TV once you load that TV's code set (provider).
analogy.breaks: Remote codes are tiny; providers carry full CRUD and diff logic.

example.title: How core runs a provider
flow: Core launches it as a child process
example.outcome: why providers are the extension point.

points: Write one for any CRUD API.

check.q: What does Terraform core delegate to providers?
check.a: Everything API-specific: schemas, reading, planning and applying create/update/delete for each resource type.

the-protocol-grpc-and-go-plugin.core: Core and providers talk via HashiCorp's go-plugin library: core starts the provider binary, they handshake over stdout with a magic cookie and protocol version, then speak gRPC (Terraform plugin protocol v5 or v6). Key RPCs are GetProviderSchema, ValidateResourceConfig, ReadResource, PlanResourceChange, ApplyResourceChange and ImportResourceState. Process isolation means a provider crash doesn't corrupt core.

first_principles.problem: A developer can't understand why their provider prints nothing when run directly.
derivation: Core **launches** the binary with env cookie.
Implement **schema, plan, apply, read, import** RPCs.
Use **protocol v6** via the Plugin Framework.

analogy.title: An interpreter at a conference
analogy.story: A booked interpreter checks a passcode, agrees on a language, then translates every request word for word.
analogy.breaks: Interpreters paraphrase; RPCs carry exact typed values.

steps.detail: Each step maps to a function you implement.

example.outcome: the contract between core and provider.

check.q: Why does running a provider binary directly do nothing useful?
check.a: It expects to be launched by core with the handshake cookie and then serve gRPC; without that it just exits or waits.

sdkv2-vs-the-plugin-framework.core: SDKv2 is the older, map-based library used by most legacy providers: schemas are map[string]*Schema and values are untyped interfaces, with null and unknown values blurred. The Terraform Plugin Framework is the modern, strongly typed library on protocol v6, with explicit null, unknown and known states, plan modifiers, validators and nested attributes. New providers should use the Framework; existing ones can migrate gradually with muxing.

first_principles.problem: An SDKv2 provider can't tell whether a user set a bool to false or left it unset, causing spurious diffs.
truths: Large providers can't rewrite at once.

analogy.title: Paper forms vs a validated web form
analogy.story: A paper form can't tell a blank from a deliberate 'no'; a typed web form records each field precisely.
analogy.breaks: Forms are filled by humans; schemas are consumed by code.

example.title: Framework schema
example.outcome: precise schemas with fewer diff bugs.

provider-project-structure.core: A provider repo usually follows the scaffolding template: main.go starts providerserver.Serve; internal/provider holds the provider (configuration schema and client setup), one file per resource and data source, and tests; examples/ and docs/ feed the registry via tfplugindocs; and GoReleaser plus GPG signing produce registry-ready releases.

first_principles.problem: A provider's resources, client code and docs are tangled in one file, making contributions painful.
truths: Registry expects a layout and signatures.
derivation: Put the **API client** in its own package.

analogy.title: A well-organised kitchen
analogy.story: Pantry (client), stations per dish (resources), recipe cards (docs) and a delivery process (releases).
analogy.breaks: Kitchens adapt freely; registries require exact naming and signatures.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Familiar layout for contributors and the registry.

check.q: Why keep the API client in a separate package?
check.a: It isolates HTTP/auth logic from Terraform types, making it reusable and testable on its own.

crud-operations.core: Each resource implements Create, Read, Update and Delete (plus optional ImportState). Create calls the API and saves the returned ID and computed attributes into state. Read refreshes state from the API and removes the resource from state if it's gone (404). Update applies in-place changes, and Delete removes it. Read must be accurate, because it drives drift detection and every plan.

first_principles.problem: A Read that ignores 404s makes Terraform think a deleted record still exists, so it never recreates it.
truths: Computed fields come from the API.
derivation: **Create**: call API, set ID and computed fields.

analogy.title: A librarian's catalogue
analogy.story: Add a card when a book arrives, check the shelf to update cards, and remove the card if the book is gone.
analogy.breaks: Librarians notice odd things; Read only knows what the API returns.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Deleted records reappear in the next plan as 'to create'.

check.q: What should Read do if the API returns 404?
check.a: Remove the resource from state so Terraform plans to recreate it.

acceptance-testing.core: Acceptance tests (resource.Test with TF_ACC=1) run real Terraform against the real API: apply a config, check attributes, change the config and check the update, test import, and check destroy. They are slower and cost money but are the only way to prove CRUD and diff logic. Unit tests cover helpers, and CheckDestroy confirms cleanup.

first_principles.problem: A provider passes unit tests but every second apply shows a perpetual diff on 'ttl'.
derivation: Run in **CI with a sandbox account**.

analogy.title: A test drive, not a brochure
analogy.story: You drive, change gears, park and return the car to be sure it really works.
analogy.breaks: Test drives are free; API calls and resources may cost money.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Framework also re-plans after each step and fails on unexpected diffs.

check.q: How do acceptance tests catch perpetual diffs?
check.a: After each apply step the framework runs another plan and fails if it isn't empty.

debugging-providers.core: Debug with logs first: TF_LOG=DEBUG (or TF_LOG_PROVIDER) plus tflog structured logging inside the provider. For deeper issues, run the provider in debug mode (Delve with -debug flag), which prints TF_REATTACH_PROVIDERS so Terraform attaches to your running process and you can set breakpoints. Dev overrides in .terraformrc point Terraform at a locally built binary without publishing.

first_principles.problem: A provider panics on update only in one user's config, and print statements don't show up.
truths: Provider stdout is the RPC channel.

analogy.title: Listening in on a phone call
analogy.story: Instead of shouting into the line (stdout), you tap the call (logs) or join it with a headset (debugger).
analogy.breaks: Phone taps are passive; breakpoints pause the provider and can time out core.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Local binary used, structured logs captured.

check.q: Why shouldn't a provider print debug output to stdout?
check.a: stdout carries the go-plugin handshake, so stray output can break communication; use tflog/stderr logs.
